items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: The most abundant enzyme on Earth is bad at its job
items.claim: Rubisco fixes carbon dioxide into sugar in every photosynthesising organism. It's the most abundant protein on the planet (about half a kilogram in every square metre of leaf). It's also slow (3 reactions per second per active site) and confuses CO2 with O2.
items.prompt: Why do plants invest so heavily in such a flawed enzyme?

options.text: There's no alternative — Rubisco is the only carbon-fixation enzyme that works

Rubisco evolved when the atmosphere had little O2; the confusion between CO2 and O2 was rare then. Now plants mass-produce it (often 50 percent of leaf protein) to compensate for its slowness, and C4 plants concentrate CO2 around it to outcompete O2 binding
Rubisco is highly efficient — the textbook is wrong

items.reveal:
Rubisco's active site binds CO2 by inserting it into a bound substrate (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate). About 25 percent of the time at room temperature, it grabs O2 instead — initiating photorespiration, a wasteful cycle that costs energy and releases CO2.

This was tolerable in the Proterozoic atmosphere (low O2, high CO2). As oxygen rose and CO2 dropped, the problem grew.

C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) evolved an extra carbon-fixation step in mesophyll cells (using PEP carboxylase, which doesn't confuse O2). This shuttles CO2 into specialised bundle-sheath cells at high concentration, where Rubisco then operates without interference.

CAM plants (cacti, pineapples) do the same trick temporally — fixing CO2 at night when stomata can be open without losing water.
items.why: Evolution doesn't engineer optimal enzymes — it tinkers around constraints inherited from earlier conditions. Rubisco is a beautiful example of a molecular legacy system.
